facts.title: Asia's First Element
facts.text: Nihonium was the first chemical element discovered in Asia, synthesized by a team led by Kosuke Morita at the RIKEN institute near Tokyo, Japan. Its name comes from "Nihon," one of the Japanese words for Japan, meaning "Land of the Rising Sun." The name and symbol Nh were officially approved by IUPAC in November 2016.

facts.title: Three Atoms in Nine Years
facts.text: Confirming nihonium's existence took extraordinary patience: the RIKEN team produced just three single atoms over nine years of experiments, in 2004, 2005, and 2012. They fired a beam of zinc-70 ions at a bismuth-209 target roughly 10 to the 19th power times, and only a handful of atoms ever fused. This made the discovery one of the most painstaking confirmations in the history of element-hunting.

facts.title: A Fleeting Existence
facts.text: Nihonium is intensely radioactive and exists for only a tiny fraction of a second. Its most stable known isotope, nihonium-286, has a half-life of about 10 seconds, while the isotopes RIKEN actually made survived for only milliseconds. Because it decays so fast, scientists identify it not by seeing the atom directly but by tracking the chain of alpha-decay products it leaves behind.

facts.title: The Long Naming Battle
facts.text: Before it had a real name, element 113 was called by the placeholder "ununtrium" (Uut), Latin-Greek for "one-one-three." A Russian-American collaboration at Dubna also claimed to have produced it, sparking a priority dispute. After review, IUPAC credited the RIKEN team with the discovery in 2015, giving Japan the honor of naming it.

facts.title: Born From Nuclear Fusion
facts.text: Nihonium is a synthetic element that does not occur anywhere in nature, on Earth or in the cosmos. It can only be created in particle accelerators by smashing lighter nuclei together so they fuse into a heavier one. This places it among the "superheavy" elements that exist solely because humans built machines powerful enough to forge them.

facts.title: Member of Element 7's Family
facts.text: Nihonium sits in group 13 of the periodic table, directly below thallium, alongside familiar elements like boron, aluminium, gallium, and indium. Chemists therefore expect it to behave loosely like a heavy post-transition metal. However, no one has ever gathered enough of it to see, weigh, or chemically test in bulk, so most of its properties are predictions rather than measurements.

facts.title: Relativity Reshapes Its Chemistry
facts.text: In superheavy atoms like nihonium, electrons whip around the nucleus at a large fraction of the speed of light, so Einstein's theory of relativity becomes important to chemistry. These relativistic effects are predicted to make nihonium's outer electrons behave unusually, possibly giving it a strong preference for the +1 oxidation state. Studying such effects is a major reason scientists bother to make these almost impossibly rare atoms.

facts.title: Hunting the Island of Stability
facts.text: Nihonium research is tied to the search for a theoretical "island of stability," a region where certain superheavy nuclei might last far longer than their neighbors. The trend in nihonium isotopes, with heavier ones living longer, offers tantalizing hints that this island could be real. Reaching it would mean creating nuclei with "magic numbers" of protons and neutrons that resist radioactive decay.

facts.title: A Predicted Heavyweight Solid
facts.text: Although it has never been seen as a visible substance, theory predicts nihonium would be a solid metal at room temperature with a high density, estimated around 16 grams per cubic centimeter, denser than lead. Calculations also suggest a melting point near 430 degrees Celsius. These figures remain purely computational, since not even a single visible speck of the metal has ever existed.

facts.title: No Job in Biology or Industry
facts.text: Nihonium has no biological role and no practical applications outside the laboratory, and it almost certainly never will. It is produced one atom at a time, costs an astronomical amount of effort to make, and vanishes within seconds. Its true value is to pure science: testing the limits of the periodic table and our understanding of how atomic nuclei and electrons behave at the extremes.
